::: {.justified}

During my time at ENSAE Paris, I volunteered weekly with **Tremplin**, an association that supports students in underprivileged high schools in the suburbs of Paris. Every week, I ran a two-hour session with *terminale* students — not just going through the syllabus, but trying to show them that mathematics is less about formulas and more about developing a way of thinking. The broader aim of the association was to give these students the confidence and the concrete tools to envision a path beyond high school — to make higher education in science feel like a realistic option rather than something reserved for others. The real challenge was rarely the content itself. It was the prior conviction many of these students had already formed about themselves: that math was not for them, that it had been decided somewhere along the way, and that no two-hour session on a Tuesday afternoon was going to change that. Sometimes it didn't. But sometimes it did, and watching a student engage genuinely with a problem they had written off an hour earlier was, without question, one of the most rewarding things I've done.

That experience confirmed something I had suspected for a long time. In another life, I would have been a teacher. Not because I enjoy standing in front of a classroom — but because I am genuinely fascinated by the moment something clicks for someone who had stopped expecting it to. I was never fully certain whether I would have ended up teaching mathematics or physics. They pull in slightly different directions. With mathematics, the ambition would have been to make people appreciate it — to dismantle the widespread and stubborn belief that it is abstract, disconnected from daily life, and useful only to a small group of specialists. That belief does real damage. Probability, logic, geometry — these are not tools reserved for academics. They are languages for thinking clearly about the world, and most people never get the chance to see them that way.

With physics, the draw was different. It was less about applications and more about the sheer strangeness of how the world actually works. My most vivid memories from *classes préparatoires* are not the problem sets or the written exams — they are the experimental sessions. My physics teacher at Lycée Clemenceau, Jean-Robert Seigne, reserved one hour every week, out of ten, entirely for experiments connected to the chapter we were studying. No grades, no pressure, just observation. A pendulum, an interference pattern, a circuit behaving in a way that contradicted what we thought we had understood. That hour felt different from everything else. It was the part of the week where physics stopped being a discipline and started being a question.

I did not become a teacher. I went to ENSAE, then to UCLA Anderson, and I am building a career in quantitative finance. But the instinct never entirely went away — the desire to explain things carefully, to find the right angle on a problem, to make something that looks impenetrable feel, eventually, obvious. The problems collected here sit at the intersection of probability, logic, and combinatorics. They are the kind of problem I find myself drawn to: the ones where the answer is never quite where you expect it, and where the interesting part is not the result but the path that gets you there. Some I encountered during my preparatory classes, some during my studies at ENSAE, some in books or in conversation. I have tried to write up the solutions in a way that makes the reasoning visible — not just the final answer, but the thinking behind it. My hope is that they are as enjoyable to read through as they were for me to work out.

:::
